conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___, one of the hospitalists. You're here tonight because your rheumatologist wanted you observed after your second rituximab infusion due to what happened last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, after the first one I got really sick—low blood pressure, blurry vision, even saw and heard things that weren’t there. I was so scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That sounds like an adrenal crisis, especially since you're on long-term steroids for your psoriatic arthritis. Your body may not be able to respond to stress like it should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So this time, they gave me the infusion earlier in the day, right? I felt that heaviness again and my vision got a bit blurry, but my blood pressure stayed okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you received the full 1000 mg slowly over five hours. Your vitals were stable throughout—no drop in blood pressure below 110 systolic, which is good. That heaviness and blurriness are similar to last time, but without dangerous drops in BP, it’s much less concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I’m still at risk? Should I always be admitted for these infusions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s something to discuss with your rheumatologist. Given your history, observation like this may be wise for future doses. We’ll make sure they know how you did tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidneys—they were affected last time too, weren’t they?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your creatinine was elevated after the first infusion, suggesting acute kidney injury, likely from low blood pressure. But your labs this morning show normal kidney function—creatinine is 1.0, which is excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my blood sugar was high again—348 this morning. I know I need to watch that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose was elevated, but that’s common in the hospital, especially with steroid use. You’re staying on your usual insulin—Levemir and NovoLog as needed—so we’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using my carb counting—5 grams per unit. And correction dose: 3 units for every 10 mg/dL over 100.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s well-managed. We’ll make sure your discharge instructions include all your insulin regimens exactly as you use them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I just reviewed your overnight vitals. Your blood pressure stayed in the 105–116 systolic range—lower than usual but stable. No symptoms, and you slept well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, slept fine. Felt a bit tired, but no dizziness or confusion. My CPAP worked well too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your oxygen levels stayed above 95% on room air. Everything looks stable—neurologically clear, heart regular, lungs clear. We’re comfortable discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no changes to my meds? I keep taking everything the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. All your home medications continue—dexamethasone, azathioprine, insulin, blood pressure meds, and the rest. No changes were made.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I see my rheumatologist in six weeks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as planned. They’ll decide if future infusions need similar monitoring. In the meantime, if you feel dizzy, confused, or very weak, go to the ER and mention your adrenal insufficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I should carry a steroid emergency card, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. And consider wearing medical alert identification. If you’re ever ill or injured, stress-dose steroids could be life-saving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for watching me so closely. I feel much better knowing I didn’t crash again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. You did well today. We’ll get your discharge papers ready, and you should be home within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Your final vitals are stable—BP 124/72, heart rate 68. You’re alert, walking fine, and tolerating food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, feeling normal. Ready to go home and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Discharge instructions are printed, including your meds and follow-up. Take care, and we hope not to see you back soon!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.
